Few names are hotter in Hollywood right now than Glen Powell, and one of his biggest movies from the last few years is finding continued success on streaming. Powell had been around for years as a supporting figure in big movies like The Dark Knight Rises, but it wasn’t until he teamed up with Tom Cruise in 2022 for Top Gun: Maverick that he truly arrived as a star. Powell’s rising stardom was called into question last year when he headlined The Running Man, the Stephen King remake written and directed by Edgar Wright. The film received middling reviews and was also one of the biggest bombs of the year. Powell has found redemption with his new TV series, Chad Powers, which has become one of the most-watched shows of the year on Hulu.

Top Gun: Maverick is easily the most successful movie of Powell’s career, and while that might be the case for a while, another of his movies that crushed at the box office was Twisters. The film is a sequel to the 1996 cult classic, Twister, starring Helen Hunt and Bill Paxton, but Lee Isaac Chung was enlisted to helm the second installment with a script from Joseph Kosinski and Mark L. Smith. If Kosinski’s name sounds familiar, it’s because he directed both Top Gun: Maverick and F1, the 2025 box office smash hit starring Brad Pitt. Now two years removed from the global premiere of Twisters in theaters, the film has found a streaming home on Hulu, but it’s also become one of the most-watched titles in the world on Prime Video. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Anthony Ramos star alongside Powell in the film.

Collider Exclusive · Action Franchise Quiz
What Action Series Would You Thrive In?
Wick · Fast · Mission · Die Hard

Four franchises. Four completely different ideas of what a hero is: the assassin with a code, the family that never leaves anyone behind, the man who does his own stunts, and the guy who simply refuses to die. Only one of them runs on your particular brand of trouble. Eight questions will tell you which one you would survive.

How does a room know you've walked into it?
Every action hero arrives differently. Some of them arrive before they arrive.

ASomeone recognises me, and the temperature in the room drops without a single word being said.
BLoudly and warmly. I arrive with my people, and we're already laughing about something.
CI'm the one who told everybody where to stand. I walked this room twice before anyone else arrived.
DBy accident. I wasn't supposed to be here, and now I'm the only one who can do anything about it.

It turns physical. What does your fighting actually look like?
Choreography is character. Yours says something about you.

AEconomical and devastating. Trained technique, no wasted motion, finished before most people notice it started.
BLoud, heavy and weirdly joyful. I'm not elegant, I hit like a truck, and I always have backup.
CTo plan, until the plan breaks. Then I improvise at full sprint and refuse to stop moving.
DBadly, honestly, and with a lot of swearing. I take more damage than I deal and I still don't go down.

Who is standing beside you when it starts?
Some franchises are built on a team. Others are built on one person walking in alone.

ANobody. I have contacts, favours and people who owe me, but when it begins I work alone.
BEveryone. My people are the entire point, and I'd trade the whole mission for any one of them.
CA small hand-picked team I trust completely, and I'd still take the worst part of the job myself.
DA voice on the other end of a radio and a building full of people who don't know I exist.

It has gone badly wrong. What keeps you upright?
Act two exists to find out what you're actually made of.

AFocus, commitment and sheer will. Grief is fuel if you point it in the right direction.
BThe people counting on me. I don't appear to have a limit when it's family on the line.
CRefusing to accept the odds. Somebody has to do the impossible part, and it's going to be me.
DSpite, mostly. And a growing sense that these people picked the wrong building.

There's a vehicle. What are you driving, and how?
No action franchise has ever survived without a car chase. This one is yours.

AA black muscle car I am unreasonably attached to, and I will dismantle an entire empire over it.
BSomething impossibly modified, at impossible speed, off an impossible ramp. Physics is a suggestion.
CA motorbike at full throttle through a city I memorised last night. And then off a cliff.
DA borrowed car, badly, while somebody in the passenger seat politely asks me to slow down.

How do you feel about the people giving the orders?
There is always an institution. There is rarely a good one.

AThere are rules and I respect them absolutely, right up until somebody breaks one against me.
BI don't take orders. I take care of people, and everything else tends to sort itself out.
CI serve the mission, not the memo. If my people are in danger, the orders come second.
DThey're in a van outside telling me what I'm doing wrong while I'm the one bleeding on broken glass.

Underneath all of it, what are you actually doing this for?
The stunts are the reason people come. This is the reason they stay.

ASomething was taken from me that can't be replaced, and I've been settling that account ever since.
BBelonging. I built a family out of people who had nowhere else, and I'll defend it with everything.
CThe conviction that if I stop, people die. I don't know how to hand that to anyone else.
DI just wanted to get through the holidays with my family. Everything after that was self-defence.

When the credits roll, what do people say about you?
Every franchise is really an argument about what makes someone worth watching.

AThat I was a myth people warned each other about in whispers, and that they were right to.
BThat I never left anyone behind, the door was always open, and there was always a place at the table.
CThat I did the impossible part myself, every single time, and never asked anyone to risk it for me.
DThat I was just a guy in the wrong place at the wrong time, who turned out to be very hard to kill.

“Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Kate Cooper, a former storm chaser haunted by a devastating encounter with a tornado during her college years who now studies storm patterns on screens safely in New York City. She is lured back to the open plains by her friend, Javi (Golden Globe nominee Anthony Ramos, In the Heights) to test a groundbreaking new tracking system. There, she crosses paths with Tyler Owens (Glen Powell), the charming and reckless social-media superstar who thrives on posting his storm-chasing adventures with his raucous crew, the more dangerous the better. As storm season intensifies, terrifying phenomena never seen before are unleashed, and Kate, Tyler and their competing teams find themselves squarely in the paths of multiple storm systems converging over central Oklahoma in the fight of their lives.”
